messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Arguments: Arguments, Uncertainty: Uncertainty
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Thea

Thea was twenty-two when the sedan crossed the centre line. She had been driving home from her parents' house in Sacramento on a clear afternoon in June, thinking about nothing in particular, when a pickup truck swerved into her lane without warning. There was no time to brake properly. The impact came on her driver's side, metal folding inward, her body thrown sideways as the car spun. She remembered the sound—a noise unlike anything she had heard before—and the sensation of losing control, of being a passenger in her own vehicle as it skidded across the asphalt. When the car finally stopped, she was still breathing. The other driver, who had been texting, walked away with minor injuries. Thea spent two nights in the hospital with a fractured collarbone and deep bruising along her ribs.

The physical injuries healed within weeks. The rest did not. By the time she married her husband Marcus three years later, Thea had constructed an elaborate architecture of avoidance that she believed was simply the way she now lived. She worked remotely as a database administrator, a job that suited her preference for minimal human contact, though her manager had begun to notice her declining participation in team meetings. When colleagues with names similar to the other driver's name appeared in her inbox or on video calls, her chest would tighten. She had come to believe that the crash had been her fault—that she had been driving too fast, or not paying enough attention, or somehow had failed to anticipate what was coming. More than that, she was certain she could have done something in those final seconds to prevent it. She would replay the moment obsessively, imagining herself swerving sooner, braking harder, as if a different Thea existed who had possessed the prescience to avoid the collision entirely. The guilt of her inaction in that moment—the fact that she had simply frozen as the truck approached—had become unbearable.

Within a year of the accident, Thea had stopped seeing friends. She told herself it was easier this way, that she was protecting them from her deteriorating mood, but the truth was more complicated. Arguments triggered something in her that felt dangerous. When Marcus raised his voice about forgotten groceries or a missed dinner, Thea's body flooded with the same helplessness she had felt in the car—the sense that something terrible was about to happen and she could not stop it. Uncertainty was perhaps worse. When Marcus mentioned that his brother might visit, or when her work schedule changed, or when a friend texted asking if she wanted to meet, Thea felt a creeping dread that something would go wrong, that she would be unable to prevent disaster. The world had become a place where terrible things happened without warning, and she was too slow, too inattentive, too fundamentally flawed to stop them.

By her twenty-fifth year, Thea had developed a method of managing the intrusive thoughts about the crash. When memories surfaced—the sound of metal, the sensation of spinning—she would pinch the inside of her forearm until it hurt, or press her fingernails into her palm. The pain created a sharp, present sensation that displaced the memory, at least temporarily. Marcus had noticed the marks on her skin but had learned not to ask. She also avoided anything that put her body under physical stress. Running made her anxious; crowded spaces made her hypervigilant; driving, even as a passenger, was nearly impossible. She had declined a promotion that would have required occasional travel.

What finally brought Thea to seek help was a moment of clarity that frightened her more than the crash itself. Marcus had suggested, gently, that they might try for a family. The thought had paralyzed her. She realized, in that moment, that she had become someone who could not trust herself to protect anyone—not even herself. She was afraid that her hypervigilance masked a fundamental incompetence, that her guilt was evidence of her culpability, and that anyone who depended on her would eventually suffer for it. She called a therapist's office on a Tuesday afternoon, her hands shaking as she gave her name.
